evidence.title: The impact of AI feedback on the accuracy of diagnosis, decision switching and trust in radiography
evidence.outcome: heatmap explanation effect on pathological accuracy
evidence.effect: Pathological cases: no AI 65.85%, heatmap 57.62%, binary feedback 72.35%; heatmap significantly decreased performance.

commentary.bottom_line: Three offline studies with physicians found that the design of AI explanations and reports changed cognitive load, task performance, and rated utility, which suggests that user testing can detect differences before deployment. No study tested whether this evaluation reduces misreading or harm in live clinical care.

perspectives.view: All three tests are level 4 and simulated. One randomized comparison of 294 ratings from 34 oncologists found evidence-graded reports rated lower in utility (mean difference -0.96; 95% CI -1.26 to -0.66). Outcomes are ratings, cognitive load, and task time rather than patient outcomes, so indirectness and small samples lower certainty.

In one hazard study, a heatmap lowered radiographer accuracy on pathological cases from 65.85% to 57.62%, while binary feedback raised it to 72.35%. Another found undesirable explanation effects for 17-35% of professionals. These results show that explanations can mislead, but they do not show that user testing prevents it.

In a study of 271 prospective physicians, explanation type changed cognitive load, task performance, and task time. Physicians rated one explanation tool at a usability score of 82/100 on 70 samples. These findings suggest that testing with target users can separate designs that fit clinical work from those that burden it, although testing took place outside real workflows.

The tests used English speech samples, German prospective physicians, and oncology physicians in unreported settings. None of them assessed how explanations are understood when patients have limited English proficiency or low literacy, or when care takes place in safety-net settings.

FDA draft guidance recommends that risks related to understanding information form part of risk management for AI-enabled devices. The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide calls for assessing whether users understand an AI solution's capabilities and limitations, and FUTURE-AI asks developers to anticipate over-reliance by end users. None of these sources sets a required testing method or comprehension threshold.

commentary.research_gap: No study has compared deployments that did and did not use clinician user testing of explanations to see whether testing reduces misinterpretation, inappropriate reliance, or patient harm in live care. Studies also have not reported how many testers or iterations are needed.
commentary.underserved_note: No test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and one test used only English speech samples. It is therefore unknown whether explanations validated in these studies are understood and acted on appropriately in settings that serve these groups.
